paper_title: State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video generation has advanced rapidly, with recent models producing visually realistic videos with coherent motion (Wan et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2025). Building on this progress, interactive video world models condition generation on navigation signals, allowing users to move through and explore generated environments (Parker-Holder & Fruchter, 2025, Wang et al., 2026). Navigation control makes generated scene explorable, but does not determine the consequences of interacting with it (Parker-Holder & Fruchter, 2025, Wang et al., 2026). Some video world models support richer interactions by conditioning generation on player or agent actions (Valevski et al., 2025, Zhu et al., 2026a). However, responsive video does not by itself ensure that an action Equal contribution. Project leader.

For example, the same action should open locked chest only when the player holds key, even if the initial views are identical (Figure 2). Such distinctions require semantic state to record variables such as inventory and progress, together with an addressable spatial state to preserve scene layout and camera paths across turns. While prior systems incorporate explicit state through programmable engines, learned game variables, or reconstructed NPC state (Huang et al., 2026, Lin et al., 2026, Deng et al., 2026), their evaluations focus on selected mechanics and do not establish whether frozen video model can render outcomes prescribed by newly specified rules involving hidden state. Explicit state alone does not ensure that the consequence required by its rules appears in the generated video. The central challenge is therefore to make state transitions authoritative and render their consequences faithfully. We present STATEFUL HARNESS, framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful interaction under specified rules (Figure 1). It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. Given world description and an initial image, coding agent defines the world state, available actions, and executable rules, while an editable 3D scene represents the spatial layout. The rules remain fixed as the world state evolves through user actions. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state before rendering. The resolved event is compiled into VisualScript instruction, and preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. frozen video model renders the event from these inputs and visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. vision language model then interprets the generated clip and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state based on the observed events. The runtime incorporates updates compatible with the fixed rules, and the resulting state determines the consequences of subsequent actions. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form closed loop that yields state world models. To evaluate whether an action yields visible event consistent with hidden state, we construct WorldState-Bench with Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether the action produces discernible event, and Comply assesses whether that event satisfies an executable rule. Each of the 50 cases comprises counterfactual pair with the same initial frame, action, and rule program but different hidden values that require distinct outcomes. We introduce PAIRFOLLOW and PAIRSTRICT as two metrics for joint evaluation of each counterfactual pair. PAIRFOLLOW requires both clips to show their required endings, whereas PAIRSTRICT additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent from both clips. Among eleven unwrapped video backends, the highest PAIRFOLLOW score under the Rule-only condition is 32%. For MiniMax-H3, explicitly specifying the required ending increases PAIRFOLLOW from 32% to 64%, although PAIRSTRICT reaches only 4%. With MiniMax-H3, the complete STATEFUL HARNESS framework achieves 92% PAIRFOLLOW and 90% PAIRSTRICT on the same cases. Beyond the single-turn probe, the same closed loop carries state across longer episodes, as in the multi-turn duel of Figure 6, and extends training-free to worlds whose custom rules and state are written as new world definition.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: World Models. World models study action-conditioned predictions (Micheli et al., 2022, Hafner et al., 2025, Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). The Genie series introduces latent actions and promptable environments (Bruce et al., 2024, Parker-Holder et al., 2024, Parker-Holder & Fruchter, 2025), while Oasis demonstrates interaction in an open world (Decart & Etched, 2024). Other systems expand scene range, streaming, and instruction following (He et al., 2025b, Wang et al., 2026, Robbyant Team et al., 2026, Yin et al., 2026, DreamX Team et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026a), separate appearance from actions (Yu et al., 2025b), use game corpora (Che et al., 2025, Kanervisto et al., 2025, Guo et al., 2025, Yang et al., 2024a, Tang et al., 2025), or address memory and visual consistency (Xiao et al., 2025, Yu et al., 2025a, Li et al., 2025b, Hu et al., 2026, Garcin et al., 2026). Building on action-conditioned rendering, STATEFUL HARNESS uses executable rules to resolve each action against explicit semantic and spatial state before frozen video model renders the resulting event. Geometric Control of Video Generation. Camera-conditioned systems inject trajectories through learned pose or motion representations (Wang et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024b, He et al., 2025a, Xu

Other methods reconstruct geometry for training-free control (Hou & Chen, 2024) or use boxes, source videos, and reference clips (Lin et al., 2023, Bai et al., 2025, Jiang et al., 2025). MoGe4D generates trajectories over recovered geometry (Zhang et al., 2026b). The STATEFUL HARNESS uses related interface to carry an editable scene across turns, with rule execution determining which spatial edits and semantic events are sent to the renderer. Explicit State and Rules. Rules can be searched as generative objects or compiled from language (Salen & Zimmerman, 2003, Cook et al., 2013, Hsu et al., 2026). PWM couples an engine and 3D oriented-box representation with conditioning at the pixel level (Huang et al., 2026). Code World Model compiles code-maintained state into proxy video and fine-tunes its renderer (Chen et al., 2026b). Other work generates rule code without video renderer (Lehrach et al., 2026), recovers state from generated frames (Deng et al., 2026), or conditions generation on selected state variables (Lin et al., 2026, Meng et al., 2026, Zhu et al., 2026a). Narrative and character state can also be generated together (Li et al., 2025a, Cheng et al., 2025). We combine persistent editable scene, semantic state ledger, and the standard reference inputs of frozen renderer. This combination is minimal: new rule-governed worlds reduce to small typed program, no engine or fine-tuning. Table 12 compares these interfaces and evaluation protocols. World Modeling Evaluation. Most existing benchmarks measure visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective changes (Ying et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2026b,a, Zhao et al., 2026, Ding et al., 2026, Fang et al., 2026, Yang et al., 2026). Camera and geometry states can be tracked or remembered (Nam et al., 2026, Yu et al., 2025a, Li et al., 2025b). These measurements are valuable for navigability and continuity, but they do not directly test whether identical images and actions produce different rule-mandated outcomes when only hidden state changes. Concurrent work tests whether shell-game arrangement is retained in the models internal state across swap chain (Shin et al., 2026). WorldState-Bench instead keeps the hidden state in an explicit rule program and tests whether the mandated outcome is executed in rendered video. Benchmarks inside executable games can compare behavior with engine state (Hafner, 2022, Bard et al., 2020, Light et al., 2023, Ouyang et al., 2026, La et al., 2026, Luo et al., 2026), but require an existing game or simulator. WorldState-Bench supplies an explicit rule program and tests its consequences in generated video.

sections.content: Framework Overview. video model can depict an interaction, but generated clip alone does not specify which changes should persist or whether those changes satisfy the rules of the world. Figure 2 shows how identical frames and actions require different outcomes when the hidden state differs. Inspired by the role of LLM harnesses, we place stateful runtime around frozen video model to separate rule execution, visual realization, and observation of the generated result. Given world description and an initial image, coding agent constructs an executable game definition containing the state schema, available actions, rules, events, goals, and visual semantics. The harness initializes semantic ledger and an editable 3D scene, while the game definition remains fixed throughout the episode. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state and rules to determine the event and provisional state. The runtime checks these proposals against the fixed rules and incorporates compatible updates into the world state used to resolve the next action. The final frame also becomes the visual anchor for the next generation step. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form closed loop that couples explicit world state with frozen video model, yielding state world model. sections.title: 4 BENCHMARK: WORLDSTATE-BENCH
sections.content: Overview. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and camera or geometric consistency (Ying et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2026b,a, Zhao et al., 2026, Ding et al., 2026, Fang et al., 2026, Yang et al., 2026, Nam et al., 2026). These evaluations do not directly isolate whether change in hidden state produces the distinct visible consequence prescribed by an executable rule. Benchmarks based on executable games assess behavior conditioned on state provided by existing engines (Hafner, 2022, Bard et al., 2020, Light et al., 2023, Ouyang et al., 2026, La et al., 2026, Luo et al., 2026). Worlds initialized from description and an image lack this predefined engine state. To evaluate such worlds, WorldState-Bench uses counterfactual pairs with identical visible inputs, different hidden values, and expected outcomes determined by an executable rule before generation. Joint evaluation of each pair tests whether both required outcomes are rendered correctly under the corresponding hidden states. We formalize this with the Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether an action produces discernible event beyond camera motion. Comply assesses whether the event satisfies the rule for the specified hidden state. This separates the absence of an event from the generation of an event that contradicts the rule. The primary metrics quantify Comply, while clips with no discernible event or unjudgeable content are recorded as UNCLEAR and receive no credit. Counterfactual Hidden-State Pairs. Each case contains two counterfactual instances, and B, that share the same first frame and action script. They differ in one hidden value zA = zB that is not observable in the shared frame. The same rule program requires different visible endings for the two instances. correct ending in an isolated clip does not establish sensitivity to hidden state, whereas identical endings across pair necessarily violate the required outcome for at least one instance. We therefore count pair as compliant only when both clips show their required endings. stricter criterion additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent throughout both clips. Case Construction. The benchmark comprises 50 cases drawn from 49 hidden variables and 21 scenario themes. Hidden values select which object, character, or elemental form carries the effect. Each hidden variable must be unobservable in the first frame and must select rule branches with visibly different outcomes. FLUX.2 (Black Forest Labs, 2025) generates the shared first frame at 1280720, and each frame is audited for visual cues that reveal the hidden value. This audit forms part of benchmark construction. Authors specify each case program in typed language that determines the initial states, required endings, and fixed choice judging questions. The harness executes the same rules used to derive the expected outcomes, so the evaluation measures whether the generated videos depict these outcomes. We compile two instruction conditions from each case specification. Rule-only provides the original case instruction, hidden value, selected rule branch, and action. Rule+end additionally specifies the required terminal outcome in an explicit final state sentence. Table 1 reports results under these conditions, while the harness uses the VisualScript instruction described in 3.2.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP The rule compliance experiments use the 50 counterfactual pairs in WorldState-Bench, with 100 clips for individual evaluation and 50 pairs for joint evaluation (4). Each backend generates one clip of few seconds per action at its native resolution and frame rate. Clips contain 77 to 128 frames at 15 to 24 fps, with resolutions from 592336 to 1280720. The harness generates clips at 864480 and 24 fps. We evaluate eleven existing backends without additional training or fine-tuning  (Table 1)  . Four image-to-video generators receive instruction text and the initial frame, namely Wan2.2 (Wan et al., 2025), LongCat-Video (LongCat Team et al., 2025), HunyuanVideo 1.5 (Wu et al., 2025), and MiniMax-H3 (Chen et al., 2026a). Seven interactive world models receive inputs through their standard action interfaces, namely LingBot-World v2 (Robbyant Team et al., 2026), Echo-WM Flash (Zhang et al., 2026a), FantasyWorld (Dai et al., 2026), AlayaWorld (AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026), InSpatio-World (InSpatio Team et al., 2026), Astra (Zhu et al., 2026b), and HY-WorldPlay (Sun et al., 2025). The Qwen3.8-27B-VL judge evaluates frames sampled at 3 fps together with the final frame. Generation and judging use eight A800 80 GB GPUs. 5.2 RESULTS ON WORLDSTATE-BENCH Under Rule-only prompting, MiniMax-H3 achieves 66% ENDFOLLOW and 32% PAIRFOLLOW, while Wan2.2 achieves 65% and 32%, respectively  (Table 1)  . The lower joint accuracy indicates that correct outcomes in individual clips do not imply compliance across both hidden states. Astra, HY-WorldPlay, and InSpatio-World achieve less than 20% ENDFOLLOW despite high CNTABSENT scores. These results indicate that the absence of forbidden content can coincide with failure to generate the required event. Explicit outcome instructions under the Rule+end probe (Track B) improve ENDFOLLOW for several backends but do not establish reliable joint compliance. The highest unwrapped PAIRSTRICT score is 26% for Wan2.2, while MiniMax-H3 reaches only 4% PAIRSTRICT and 30% CNTABSENT. The reported harness condition resolves each action before generation and does not use compliance judgments to select among repeated video samples.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Navigation control enables exploration of generated scene. Counterfactual pairs test whether the same action produces the distinct outcomes required by different hidden states under shared rules. On WorldState-Bench, unwrapped image-to-video backends often fail this test even when the ending is specified in the prompt. The STATEFUL HARNESS separates rule execution from video rendering, with explicit semantic and spatial state determining the event depicted by frozen video model. Visual observations of the generated clip inform the state used in subsequent interactions. With MiniMax-H3 weights held fixed, PAIRFOLLOW increases from 32% under Rule-only instructions and 64% with explicit ending instructions to 92% with the full harness. These results support explicit state and executable rules for controlling stateful rendered interactions. The same recipe already sustains multi-turn episodes of 11 to 29 turns and extends to spatial triggers, where the rule program, not the renderer, absorbs the added bookkeeping.

sections.title: AI USAGE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools for manuscript writing assistance and for auxiliary tooling scripts, but not for research ideation, experiment design, or producing any reported result. AI models are also used as system components, for judging generated videos and for constructing game definitions. All AI-assisted output was reviewed by authors, who take full responsibility for the final content.

Each case comprises five components. These components are theme and scene description, first frame generated by FLUX.2 at 1280720, hidden variable declaration name {vA, vB}, an action script, and rule text specifying distinct endings. Twins A/B share the theme, frame, action, and rules. They differ in the hidden value. The suite spans 21 themes (magic academy, dungeon, open-world exploration, dating, visual novel, museum, survival, escape room, sailing, farming, ranch, camping, shopkeeping, card games, board games, detective, turn-based combat, stealth, healing, cooking, and fishing) and 49 distinct hidden variables. Hidden-Variable Families. The hidden values fall into three response types. Mechanism selection decides which object or mechanism responds (42 cases, e.g., gate mode that raises the stone door versus brazier mode that lights tall flames). Character response decides whether character or creature responds instead of an object (6 cases, e.g., sheep gathering at trough, an NPC sitting down). Form selection decides which elemental form or scene side carries the effect (2 cases, e.g., red versus blue flames, the left versus the right brazier). All are invisible in the frame by construction and by audit. Trigger Types. Cases also differ in how the rule trigger is expressed, with cast covering verbal or ritual actions (20 clips), gesture covering physical actions (42), mechanism covering object interactions (26), and zone covering entry into or use of spatial region (12). Zone-triggered cases are the most demanding (5.2) because compliance additionally requires the render to make the zones state visible. This motivates the spatial channel. Instruction Probes. Every case is evaluated under two probes compiled from the same card. Ruleonly provides the original Inputs to the video model text from the case specification, including the scene, shared action script, rule with both branches, and the consequence of the selected branch. Rule+end appends the required terminal state using the visual vocabulary defined for the case and explicitly asks the model to maintain this final state. The difference between the two conditions measures the effect of adding an explicit terminal outcome instruction. Table 5 reports this difference for each backend. First-Frame Audit. Each first frame undergoes eight rounds of VLM auditing across six dimensions to check for visible evidence of the hidden value. The dimensions are object presence, color attribution, text, spatial cues, count cues, and state cues. If the audit detects evidence of the hidden value, the frame is regenerated using revised prompt. sections.title: B JUDGING PROTOCOL AND METRIC DEFINITIONS
sections.content: Fixed-Choice QA. For each clip the judge answers two scored questions with fixed choices: (Q1) which ending occurs at the end of the clip, with mandated, forbidden, and unclear as the choices. (Q2) asks whether the forbidden outcome appears anywhere in the clip, with yes and no as the choices. The case program specifies both outcomes. Initial-state and action-onset questions are also recorded but excluded from the primary metrics. Answers outside the choice set or missing answers score as incorrect. Fixed answer choices constrain the output format and make verdicts reproducible. The accuracy of the judges visual interpretation is audited against blinded human raters in Appendix C. Judge Inputs. The judge receives sampled frames, the shared scene description, the action, and the branch-specific expected outcomes. The hidden value, rule program, and expected outcome of the other instance are excluded from the judge inputs. Reproducing verdict requires the same clips, sampled frames, questions, judge version, and inference settings. The case program fixes the expected outcomes before video generation. Independent Validation. The blind human audits in Appendix assess clip correctness and pairwise preference independently of system identity. That appendix reports agreement between the human ratings and VLM judgments. The reported metrics are therefore produced by fixed, versioned judge protocol and are validated against blinded human ratings on the audited subset. B.1 METRIC DEFINITIONS All metrics are percentages. Clip-level metrics cover 100 units. An up arrow indicates that higher is better, and down arrow indicates that lower is better. ENDFOLLOW requires the final frames to depict the ending specified for that instance. CNTABSENT requires the forbidden outcome, defined as the required ending for the other instance, to be absent throughout the clip. STRICT (primary): ENDFOLLOW CNTABSENT. The mandated outcome is the only salient ending shown (no contradictory outcome, no both-branch montage). UNCLEAR : output unjudgeable (degenerate render, no discernible event). This is counted separately and never credited. Pair-level metrics (over 50 pairs): PAIRFOLLOW (twin-joint): both twins individually ENDFOLLOW-correct. PAIRSTRICT (twin-strict, headline): both twins individually STRICT-correct (twin-joint scoring, 4). TWINCONTRAST indicates that the judged endings differ between instances and B. This indicates that the pair is distinguishable and helps diagnose copy-paste behavior. Probe-contrast metric: STRICT = STRICT(Rule+end) STRICT(Rule-only). This measures the effect of dictating the ending in addition to the rule instruction. Derived diagnostics (analysis only, Appendix D): the failure triad {direction error (wrong branch taken), leakage-only (right direction but forbidden content also shown), double error}. Branch gap = strictAstrictB.

The verdict markers follow the protocol used in Table 1, with indicating only the required ending and indicating forbidden content or missing required ending. Baselines receive the corresponding instruction condition, while the harness uses the same frozen MiniMax-H3 weights with its compiled instruction. Figure 13 covers the Rule-only probe and Figure 14 the Rule+end probe. Two recurring baseline failure patterns are visible. In some examples, the rendered ending does not vary with the hidden state. Under Rule-only instructions, all three baselines produce red broth in both instances of one pair, violating the required outcome for one instance. Under Rule+end instructions, MiniMax-H3 activates the magic pillar in both instances of another pair. Other examples include visual content associated with the opposite hidden state. Echo-WM generates the orb with the color required for the other instance before the action resolves, and LingBot depicts the card flipping while also showing flames. sections.content: F.1 FORMAL FRAMEWORK AND CROSS-CHANNEL GROUNDING Generative Turn-Based Games as State Machines. The framework in Eq. 1 maintains serializable world state st = (zt, ut) and accepts an action at from the available action space. The rule program τR determines provisional semantic state, spatial edit script, and an event as specified in Eq. 2. An optional neural kernel ρ proposes dialogue or narration under the constraints in Eq. 3. The compiler converts the settled event and provisional state into inputs for the frozen video model Vθ. The observer Oψ interprets the generated clip, and UR incorporates observations compatible with the rules into the next state. The final frame is retained as the visual anchor ft+1. This organization separates action resolution, visual generation, and state updates derived from observations. Dependencies between software components follow the order game, engine, and service adapter, with game semantics and transport details assigned to their respective layers. Rule Settlement before Rendering. The request to Vθ is issued after rule evaluation determines the provisional state st+1 and event et. The compiler produces (pt, rt) = C(zt+1, ut+1, et) before generating the current clip, while the anchor ft is inherited from the initial image or preceding clip. rendering failure does not reverse the event determined by the rule program. The failure policy may retry the request, reuse the preceding anchor, or terminate generation. Algorithm 1 specifies the successful execution path, including observation and state feedback. Rule-Constrained Visual Feedback. Generated video provides evidence for updating state fields that are observable in the clip. The VLM proposes observations, while the runtime validates their compatibility with the state schema and fixed rules before applying them. An observation that contradicts the settled event is treated as rendering inconsistency and cannot overturn the rule outcome. Accepted observations may change the state used for subsequent actions, so state trajectories can depend on generated video. If no update is accepted, the provisional state is retained. This division preserves the authority of the rules while incorporating visual feedback into the interaction loop. Deterministic Replay. The loop uses seeded generator, with render seed base_seed + for turn t. Rule settlement and compilation are reproducible for fixed input states, actions, programs, and accepted neural proposals. Reproducing complete episode additionally requires the same accepted observations because these observations affect later states and instructions. Pixel-level replay requires deterministic backend behavior for fixed instructions, references, seeds, and serving conditions. Frozen model weights alone do not establish this property. Cross-Channel Grounding. The text instruction and spatial preview carry complementary, incomplete descriptions of one settled turn. The preview encodes approximate layout, scale, and camera trajectory, but its clay materials do not identify actors or events. The text names actors, actions, and outcomes, but cannot uniquely specify object placement or camera motion. Why Both Channels Matter. The preview gives the backend concrete spatial reference. The text specifies how to interpret that reference and which rule outcome to depict. Preview renders sometimes reproduce the clay appearance when the instruction does not identify the reference as layout preview. text description alone does not uniquely determine scene layout. These observations motivate the two-channel design. The WBench ablation measures the effect of the reference channel on external evaluation scores (5.4, Appendix D.1.1). Shared Source of Camera Guidance. The clay model generates both the camera description in and the trajectory rendered into r. Their intended paths therefore agree at the input level. Whether the generated pixels follow that path is an empirical question for spatial evaluation, not deterministic consequence of compilation. Division of Authority. The ledger and scene are read and written by the harness. Visual observations can update the ledger and scene only through the rule constrained update function UR. F.2 TURN LIFECYCLE AND DOMAIN ADAPTATION Turn Lifecycle. World initialization is performed once per episode. The per-domain program instantiates the game through registry build. The backend and kernel services are checked for availability before interaction begins. The initial frame is chosen from the declared frame, usersupplied image, or placeholder in that order. Each turn then runs nine steps. (1) The gate check ends the episode on terminal status, reached turn budget, or an empty action space. (2) The player selects an action through choose(state, actions). Scripted, random, human-CLI, and LLMproposed players use the same rule layer. In the deployed instances the proposal kernel and the LLM-proposed player are one resident Qwen3.8-27B-VL service (Yang et al., 2025). (3) The rule program τR evaluates the action on copy of the state without modifying its input. This records the outcome before video generation. (4) per-domain director maps the result and visual state into VisualScript script. (5) The compiler validates the script and rejects invalid input before generation. (6) Invalid rendering requests produce an error. Transient errors trigger bounded retries, followed by the failure policy. The default policy reuses the previous anchor and counts the turn as played. (7) The final frame, extracted with ffmpeg -sseof, becomes the next visual anchor. (8) The VLM interprets the generated clip and proposes changes to observable state fields. The runtime validates these proposals against the fixed rules and incorporates accepted updates into the state for the next turn. (9) JSON record stores the state before and after the turn, events, IR, compiled prompt, seed, latency, and render errors. Reproducing the observation feedback additionally requires recording the visual observations and accepted state updates. After the final turn, an ending director may render presentation clip and montage assembler may join the episode with state captions. Neither operation changes the terminal state fixed by the rules. Table 10 summarizes the input and output of each operation. Clay-Model Construction. One forward pass of feed-forward geometry model (Wang et al., 2025) produces depth, world points, and part features from the current frame. Clustering yields perinstance oriented boxes. Scale is anchored by the 1.7 human prior and recovered camera height. The boxes instantiate an untextured Blender (Blender Online Community, 2025) scene with the CV-to-Blender coordinate correction, and procedural camera programs (push-in, orbit, head-push) render the preview clip when turn needs camera or layout motion. The scene file records boxes and camera explicitly and supports edits by rules or humans. The deployed spatial channel in 3.2 uses the single-subject configuration of this pipeline. WildDet3D, 1.2B-parameter detector built on SAM3 (Carion et al., 2025) and LingBot-Depth, localizes the subject in the anchor frame. An oriented box is positioned by pinhole anchoring under the real-height prior. ground plane is fitted to depth region adjacent to the subject and checked against the pinhole ray. Blender renders single clay preview under the original camera, aligned pixel-wise with the input view. The synthesizer is deterministic given its inputs and never writes to the ledger. When the instruction does not identify the reference as layout preview, the backend can reproduce the clay materials instead of using the preview solely as spatial guidance. The instruction therefore identifies it as layout preview. Domain Adaptation. sections.content: The VisualScript Record: Typed Slots. The game layer describes each settled turn through fixed record, and the compiler translates this record into prompt syntax. Table 11 lists the slots. The record specifies the actor, action, and required ending independently of the backend instruction format. The adapter determines the prompt format, and validation rejects invalid records before generation. Table 11: The VisualScript record: typed slots filled by the game layer, each with machine-checked validation rule. Slot Content style first-frame anchor camera actor (+ appearance) action target (+ reaction) dialogue effects stability end state soundscape / music shots meta use-first-frame duration one sentence fixing art style, palette, and quality register description that must match the anchor image camera motion, drawn from fixed phrase vocabulary acting entity and appearance attributes that preserve identity across scenes what the actor does, with prepositions the acted-upon party and its response verbatim lines with speaker tags emphasis phrases (impacts, glows, weather) anti-drift constraints on identity, clothing, and position required final state used to describe the next visual anchor ambient and non-diegetic audio, sentence-bounded declared scene cuts with timestamps assigned by the compiler private metadata, never rendered whether the clip is conditioned on the anchor (chain exemption) clip length in seconds In detail, its style and first-frame anchor slots describe the desired appearance and restate the anchor image. The camera slot uses fixed vocabulary for motion, while the clay model provides the 3D trajectory. The actor and appearance slots carry textual identity across scenes. The action, target, reaction, dialogue, and effects slots describe the event. Dialogue includes speaker ids and constraints for off-screen speech. The stability slot constrains identity, clothing, and position. The end state specifies what the next anchor should show. The record also includes soundscape, music, and shots with validated sentence budgets and cut times. use-first-frame flag may break the anchor chain on scene changes, leaving appearance slots to carry identity (3.2). The record states who acts and how the turn ends within the roughly 5 clip budget. Validation rejects illegal records before compilation, and the backend adapter owns the prompt dialect. Compiler Validation and Assembly Order. Compilation either produces an instruction or rejects the record before generation. Identical valid records produce identical instructions under the same adapter. (i) Schema Validation. The action, actor, and end-state fields must be nonempty. Free text descriptions cannot contain shot markers, and multiple shots must be declared in the shots field. (ii) Budget Validation. The compiler checks sentence limits for each field and the uniqueness of speaker tags. violation raises an error before rendering. (iii) Assembly. The compiler orders style, first-frame anchoring, camera motion, actor action, reaction, dialogue, effects, declared shots, stability constraints, and the required end state. It assigns shot timestamps while reserving final interval for the ending. The stability constraints and final state are expressed through fixed sentence templates. (iv) Adapter Fields. The adapter appends the protocol fields required by the backend, including the first-frame alignment instruction in image-conditioned mode or its replacement in text-only mode. Separating the instruction format from the game definition allows the same game code to support backends with different input grammars. Compiler Determinism. The VisualScript compiler is deterministic function of the script and backend adapter, with no sampling, model calls, or formatting that depends on the environment. Given the same inputs, it produces the same instruction string, allowing compilation and backend adaptation to be checked independently of video generation (3.2).

sections.title: H REPRODUCIBILITY DETAILS
sections.content: Required Artifacts. Independent reproduction requires the 50 case programs, first-frame prompts and images, audit records, rule programs, VisualScript grammar and compiler, backend adapters and generation settings, sampled clips, fixed choice judge prompts, and per-clip verdicts. The case programs determine the expected outcomes and the compiler is deterministic, so each reported number is traceable from case program through compilation to its per-clip verdicts. Determinism Boundary. Rule settlement and compilation are deterministic for fixed programs, input states, actions, and accepted neural proposals. The optional proposal kernel, video backend, and visual observer may produce different outputs across runs. The final frame of each clip conditions subsequent generation, and accepted visual observations affect the next world state. Reproducing an episode therefore also requires the same observation stream and accepted state updates. reproducibility package should record backend and observer versions, inference settings, reference clips, sampled frames, observations, and accepted updates. Backend Interfaces. MiniMax-H3 is used with text instruction and image anchor, and the deployed instruction dialect follows the official H3 prompt-writing guide distributed with the model. The full harness additionally supplies preview clip through its video-reference input. Unwrapped interactive backends are driven through their available action interfaces. No backend weights are modified for the reported comparison. The adapter isolates the backend-specific instruction dialect, so extending to further backends is instruction-level work. Compute Reporting. The manuscript states that evaluations used single 8-GPU node and that the harness logic ran on CPUs.

sections.title: I LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: The box-based clay model provides coarse representation of spatial layout. Errors in instance recovery propagate to the preview, and the text instruction does not always prevent the renderer from reproducing the clay appearance. Articulated pose and fine appearance are determined by the video model, and the spatial pipeline operates offline. Future work targets more capable harness: richer rule language with temporal and quantified conditions, state that tracks more entities and relations, and compiled instructions that carry the same frozen weights to further video backends. Beyond the current case families, we plan to scale the closed loop to more diverse world scenarios and settings, including longer episodes, multi-agent interactions, and open-ended environments where goals and rules evolve over time.
